headline: Trenbolone was tested
body: Four weeks, young rats, femur and humerus measured.
punch: The bones came out shorter. Not longer.

headline: This compound appears
body: Usually justified by mechanism — aromatase inhibition, IGF-1 sensitivity, delayed closure. All of it reasoning forward from receptor biology.

headline: The measurement
body: Femur and humerus in young rats after four weeks, across four groups: trenbolone, exercise, trenbolone plus exercise, and control.
punch: The endpoint people actually care about.

headline: The result
body: Trenbolone shortened femur and humerus length — though the difference did not reach statistical significance in this study.
punch: Not proof of harm. Definitely not evidence of benefit.

headline: And on bone structure
body: No significant differences in bone corpus thickness, cortex thickness or medullary diameter between any of the four groups.

headline: Which is worth stating
body: A study looked for effects on growing bone and found no benefit, with the length trend pointing the wrong way. That is a different finding from 'we don't know'.

headline: The mechanism argument
body: Receptor-level reasoning predicts what could happen. Measuring the bone tells you what did. When they disagree, the measurement is not the weaker evidence.
punch: Plausible mechanisms lose to measured outcomes.

headline: The limits
body: Rat study, four weeks, underpowered for the length difference. It doesn't demonstrate shortening in humans — and nothing here supports the height claim either.
punch: Weak evidence against. No evidence for.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
